meta.titre: Geological Maps: Reading Outcrops, Dips and Faults

sections.contenu_markdown: Before a road is cut through a hillside, a dam is built or a quarry is opened, a geologist studies a geological map: a map of the ground surface on which each colour or pattern shows the rock found there, and symbols give the strike and dip of the beds. With a map, a ruler and a pencil you can decide which rocks are older and which younger, whether the rocks have been folded or faulted, and where a layer lies underground. At Advanced Level you must do this in structured questions, and you must recognise the main structures from a small sketch map in multiple choice questions.

items: Contour lines join points of equal height, and closely spaced contours mean a steep slope.
In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary beds the oldest bed is at the bottom and the youngest at the top (the principle of superposition).
A fold is a bend in layered rock, and a fault is a fracture along which the rock on one side has moved relative to the other.
On a map of scale 1:25 000, 1 cm on the map represents 25 000 cm, which is 250 m on the ground.

sections.titre: Strike, dip, outcrop patterns and the main structures on a geological map
sections.contenu_markdown:
A geological map shows the **outcrop** (the rock exposed at the ground surface) of each rock unit on a topographic base. Read the key first, then work from the oldest rock to the youngest.

### Strike and dip
**Dip** is the maximum angle, measured from the horizontal, at which a bed slopes, and the dip direction is the direction in which it slopes down. **Strike** is the direction of a horizontal line on the surface of the bed, and it lies at $90^\circ$ to the dip direction. The map symbol has a long line for strike, a short tick towards the dip direction and a number for the dip angle.

### Outcrop patterns

| Attitude of the bed | Pattern on the map |
|---|---|
| Horizontal | boundaries run parallel to the contour lines, and younger rocks cap the higher ground |
| Vertical | boundaries are straight lines along the strike and ignore the relief |
| Dipping | boundaries cut across the contours and form V shapes where they cross valleys; the V points in the direction of dip, except where beds dip downstream at an angle smaller than the slope of the valley floor, when it points upstream |

Gentle dips give wide outcrops and strongly curved boundaries; steep dips give narrow, nearly straight outcrops. On level ground the outcrop width $w$, true thickness $t$ and dip $\delta$ are related by $t = w\sin\delta$.

### Folds and relative age
In an undisturbed sequence that is the right way up, beds dip towards the younger rocks. In an **anticline** the oldest rocks lie in the core and the limbs dip away from the axis; in a **syncline** the youngest rocks lie in the core and the limbs dip towards the axis. The outcrops are repeated on either side of the axial line. A feature that cuts another is younger: a dyke, an intrusion or a fault is younger than every rock it cuts.

### Order of work for any question
1. Read the key, scale and north arrow.
2. Identify the rock types, their relative ages and their dips.
3. Look for structures: folds, faults, unconformities and intrusions.
4. Support every conclusion with evidence taken from the map.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must name the type of a fault shown on a map or in a sketch.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
The **hanging wall** is the block above an inclined fault plane and the **footwall** is the block below it.

| Fault | Movement | Typical dip | Cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | hanging wall moves down | usually steep | tension (stretching) |
| Reverse | hanging wall moves up | steeper than about $45^\circ$ | compression |
| Thrust | hanging wall moves up and over | low, less than about $45^\circ$ | strong compression |
| Tear (strike-slip, wrench) | blocks slide horizontally past each other | vertical or near vertical | shearing |

Clues on the map:
1. **Shape of the trace.** A straight trace that ignores the relief means a steep or vertical plane (normal, reverse or tear). A winding trace that follows the contours and makes V shapes in valleys means a low-angle plane, such as a thrust.
2. **Which side shows older rocks.** In a dip-slip fault the upthrown side usually exposes the older rocks, so the side that shows the younger rocks is usually the downthrown side. A thrust places older rocks on top of younger ones.
3. **Sideways displacement.** Beds, dykes or veins shifted horizontally along a straight trace, with the same sequence of rocks on both sides, point to a tear fault. Check the dips first, because dipping beds can also look shifted sideways when a dip-slip fault cuts them.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you are asked to identify an unconformity or to describe the geological history shown on a map.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
An **unconformity** is a surface of erosion or non-deposition that separates younger rocks from older rocks, so a time gap is present.

- **Angular unconformity**: younger beds rest on older beds that have been tilted or folded and eroded; the two sets have different strike and dip. On the map the older outcrops run up to the boundary and are cut off by it, and the younger rocks overlap several different older units. A basal conglomerate often lies on the surface.
- **Disconformity**: younger and older beds are parallel, so the gap shows only by an erosion surface or by missing fossil zones.
- **Nonconformity**: sedimentary rocks rest on eroded igneous or metamorphic rocks.

To write the geological history list the events in order from the oldest: deposition, folding or tilting, erosion, deposition of the next series, intrusion, faulting, and present-day erosion. Use cross-cutting relationships: whatever is cut is older than what cuts it.

variantes.nom: Calculations: scale, dip, thickness and depth
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives distances, heights or angles and asks for numerical answers.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
- **Ground distance** $=$ map distance $\times$ scale denominator.
- **True dip** from two strike lines (structure contours): $\tan\delta = \dfrac{\text{height difference}}{\text{horizontal distance at right angles to strike}}$.
- **True thickness** on level ground: $t = w\sin\delta$, with $w$ measured at right angles to the strike.
- **Depth** of a bed below a point at a horizontal distance $x$ down dip from the outcrop: $x\tan\delta$ (level ground).
- **Apparent dip** $\alpha$ in a direction making an angle $\theta$ with the strike: $\tan\alpha = \tan\delta\,\sin\theta$. It is always less than the true dip, except in the direction of dip where they are equal.

sections.enonce_markdown: The ground is level at 300 m above sea level. The top of a sandstone bed crops out along a straight line at this level, and a borehole shows the top of the same bed at 200 m above sea level at another place. On a map of scale 1:25 000 the strike line through the outcrop and the strike line through the borehole are parallel and 2.0 cm apart, measured at right angles to the strike, and the bed dips from the outcrop towards the borehole. The whole sandstone bed crops out as a band 3.0 cm wide, measured at right angles to the strike. Calculate (a) the true dip, (b) the true thickness of the sandstone, and (c) the depth of the top of the sandstone below a point on the ground 800 m from the outcrop line of its top, in the direction of dip.

etapes.action: Convert the map distance between the two strike lines to a ground distance.
etapes.justification: Ground distance = map distance x scale denominator.

etapes.action: Find the height difference between the strike lines.
etapes.justification: Each strike line joins points of equal height on the top of the bed: 300 m at the outcrop and 200 m at the borehole.
The distance was measured at right angles to the strike, so $\tan\delta$ is the height difference divided by that distance.

etapes.action: Calculate the true thickness of the bed.
etapes.justification: The outcrop width is $3.0 \times 25\,000 = 75\,000$ cm $= 750$ m, and on level ground $t = w\sin\delta$.

etapes.action: Calculate the depth 800 m down dip.
etapes.justification: The top of the bed falls by $\tan\delta$ metres for every metre travelled down dip, and the ground stays level.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Fall $= 800 \times 0.200 = 160\ \mathrm{m}$. The top of the sandstone is at $300 - 160 = 140$ m above sea level and the ground is at 300 m, so the depth is $160\ \mathrm{m}$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a) The dip is $11.3^\circ$. (b) The true thickness is about 147 m. (c) The top of the sandstone lies 160 m below the surface at that point.** The width of the band on the map (750 m) is much more than the thickness because the bed dips gently.

items.erreur_markdown: The strike of a bed is the direction in which it dips.
items.pourquoi_faux: Strike and dip are measured at right angles to each other.
items.correction_markdown: Strike is the direction of a horizontal line on the bed; the dip direction is $90^\circ$ from the strike, in the direction the bed slopes down.

items.erreur_markdown: A wide outcrop always means that a bed is thick.
items.pourquoi_faux: The width depends on the dip and on the slope of the ground as well as on the thickness. A gently dipping thin bed can have a wide outcrop.
items.correction_markdown: Use $t = w\sin\delta$ on level ground, with the width measured at right angles to the strike.

items.erreur_markdown: Beds dip towards the older rocks.
items.pourquoi_faux: In a sequence that is the right way up the beds dip towards the younger rocks, because younger beds lie on top of older ones.
items.correction_markdown: Check the dip arrows and the key: in an undisturbed sequence the age decreases in the dip direction.

items.erreur_markdown: Any line that separates two rock types on a map is a fault.
items.pourquoi_faux: A boundary may be an ordinary depositional contact, an intrusive contact or an unconformity.
items.correction_markdown: Call it a fault only when the evidence shows displacement: a straight trace cutting the structures, offset beds or a dyke, or rocks of unrelated age placed side by side.

items.erreur_markdown: The apparent dip measured on a section line is the true dip of the bed.
items.pourquoi_faux: The true dip is measured at right angles to the strike. In any other direction the slope looks smaller.
items.correction_markdown: Use $\tan\alpha = \tan\delta\,\sin\theta$ to relate apparent dip $\alpha$ and true dip $\delta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the section line and the strike.

items.enonce_markdown: Four rock units A (oldest), B, C and D (youngest) are found along an east-west line across a region with level ground. From west to east the units crop out in the order C, B, A, B, C. The beds at the western end dip west and the beds at the eastern end dip east. Name the structure, say where its axis lies, and state the dip direction of the limbs.
items.solution_markdown:
The oldest unit A lies in the core, with younger units on both sides, and the beds dip away from the middle. The structure is an **anticline**.

Its **axis lies in the outcrop of unit A**, in the middle of the traverse. The **west limb dips west and the east limb dips east** (away from the axis), and the pattern of outcrops is repeated on either side.

items.enonce_markdown: A bed dips at $30^\circ$ towards the east. (a) A cross-section line runs at $45^\circ$ to the strike. Calculate the apparent dip of the bed on this line. (b) On level ground the outcrop of the bed is 600 m wide, measured at right angles to the strike. Calculate its true thickness.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\tan\alpha = \tan 30^\circ \times \sin 45^\circ = 0.5774 \times 0.7071 = 0.4082$, so $\alpha = \mathbf{22.2^\circ}$. This is less than the true dip of $30^\circ$, as expected.

(b) $t = w\sin\delta = 600 \times \sin 30^\circ = 600 \times 0.5 = \mathbf{300\ m}$.

items.enonce_markdown: A map shows the following. A series X of limestone and shale strikes north-south and dips $40^\circ$ east. A series Y of conglomerate and sandstone strikes east-west and dips $10^\circ$ south, and its basal conglomerate lies across the cut-off edges of the beds of X. A vertical dolerite dyke cuts both X and Y. A fault displaces the dyke, the series X and the series Y, but is not displaced by anything. (a) Name the surface between X and Y. (b) List the events in order from oldest to youngest. (c) Give the evidence for the order of the last two events.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The surface between X and Y is an **angular unconformity**: the older series X is tilted and its beds are cut off, and the series Y above has a different strike and dip.

(b) Order, oldest first: **1.** deposition of X; **2.** tilting of X (dip $40^\circ$ east) and erosion; **3.** deposition of Y on the eroded surface (unconformity); **4.** intrusion of the dolerite dyke; **5.** faulting.

(c) The dyke cuts both X and Y, so it is younger than both. The fault displaces the dyke, so the fault is younger than the dyke. The fault is not displaced by anything, so it is the youngest event (cross-cutting relationships).

items_markdown: Dip is the maximum slope of a bed and strike is a horizontal line on the bed at right angles to the dip direction.
Horizontal beds follow the contours, vertical beds give straight outcrops, and dipping beds form V shapes that point in the direction of dip (with one exception for gentle downstream dips).
In a sequence that is the right way up, beds dip towards younger rocks; an anticline has the oldest rocks in its core and a syncline the youngest.

Identify faults from the trace (straight or winding), the side with the older rocks and the sideways offset; angular unconformities show cut-off older beds under younger beds with a different strike and dip.
Calculations: ground distance $=$ map distance $\times$ scale; $\tan\delta = $ height difference over horizontal distance; $t = w\sin\delta$; $\tan\alpha = \tan\delta\sin\theta$.
A feature that cuts another is younger, so list the events from the oldest using cross-cutting relationships.
